text: The example's live acceptance brings the whole market up in a throwaway state directory and exits non-zero unless every workload is up and reachable. It is bash with set -euo pipefail; ACCEPT_ROOT (default a fresh mktemp -d) is the one directory it owns, and an EXIT trap stops everything it started and removes that directory, never stopping or touching a kcp, kine or OpenBao it did not start. It asks the kernel for three free 127.0.0.1 ports, for kcp, kine and OpenBao, instead of pinning any, so it cannot collide with another instance on the machine. It starts kcp with ROOT under ACCEPT_ROOT and KCP_SECURE_PORT and KINE_ENDPOINT set to two of those ports through deploy/start-kcp.sh, installs the provider through deploy/install-provider.sh, builds ./cmd/deno-kcp-provider into ACCEPT_ROOT, starts OpenBao with OPENBAO_DIR under ACCEPT_ROOT and OPENBAO_LISTEN on the third port through deploy/start-openbao.sh, and runs the provider with --kubeconfig, --openbao-addr, --openbao-token root and RUNS_DIR under ACCEPT_ROOT. It then runs the example's apply.sh with ORG_ROOT the repository parent, KUBECONFIG the kcp admin kubeconfig, the same OPENBAO_LISTEN, START_OPENBAO=0, a bounded WAIT_SECONDS, and the key files under ACCEPT_ROOT. When apply.sh returns, whether it succeeded or not, it reads every DenoPod from kcp with kubectl and prints one line per check with its result and the decisive evidence: apply.sh exited 0; DenoPod plc in root:global, relay in root:relay, pds in root:alice, pds in root:bob and bidder in root:bob each reached phase Running and report ready true; DenoPod verifier in root:alice reached the terminal phase Succeeded; bob's pds answers on its own name, which the provider proves with its readiness probe through the shim and the host proves by fetching the same path from outside with curl against the host port; the bidder answers on its cluster-local name and on its host port. The host check names the scheme the listener actually speaks: the bob PDS serves TLS because its supervisor writes the injected leaf and appends the TLS flags, so its host check is https, and the bidder serves plain HTTP because its supervisor must not append those flags, so its host check is http; the provider's readiness probe is the one that does not care, because it tries https and then http. The five long-running pods are still Running with ready true when they are read a second time at least ten seconds later, so a pod that dies after startup fails the run. It prints a final table naming every check and its result, prints the tail of the provider log and the status of the failing pod when a check fails, and exits 0 only when every check passed.

label: SpecRequirement
text: The live acceptance must survive a provider that comes up, logs that it is waiting for its APIExport virtual workspace endpoints, and then reconciles nothing: every object apply.sh applies stays without a status and apply.sh fails on its first wait. After the provider is started and apply.sh returns, the acceptance must detect that state within a bounded window - no OpenBao object in any workspace carries status.ready true and no DenoPod exists in any workspace - and, when no workload exists yet, stop the provider, start it again, and run apply.sh again. It must make at least two and at most three attempts, print which attempt it is on, and record each attempt's apply.sh exit code. It must never restart the provider once a DenoPod exists, because the workloads are children of the provider and stopping it would orphan them.

text: apply.sh must not create the verifier after a fixed sleep. It must instead wait, with the same bounded WAIT_SECONDS deadline it uses elsewhere, until the peers the verifier reaches are observable - DenoPod pds in root:alice reports phase Running and ready true, which is the provider's own proof that pds.default.alice.svc.kcp.local resolves through the virtual DNS table and answers on /xrpc/_health - and only then apply the verifier manifest. label: SpecRequirement
text: The live acceptance's EXIT trap must stop the workloads before it stops the provider that owns them. The DenoPod processes are children of the provider, so killing the provider orphans them and they keep holding the fixed host ports 2583 to 2587 of the example, which makes the next run on the same machine unable to bind them. The trap therefore deletes every DenoPod in every workspace through kcp first, waits, bounded, for the objects to disappear (the denopod.deno.computer/run finalizer is what stops each process, and it only runs while the provider is up), and only then stops the provider, OpenBao and kcp and removes ACCEPT_ROOT. intent: This context exists to pin down the deploy/examples/atproto/market example as an executable specification of what the kcp deno runtime must support: peer services that reach each other only by cluster-local name over TLS, with identity and certificates supplied from outside the pod. It is the reference topology that exercises workspace creation, per-workspace API bindings, per-workspace RBAC, per-workspace OpenBao authority selection, the provider's virtual DNS table and shim, and the TLS leaf injection path, so that a regression in any of those surfaces shows up as a failing verifier pod rather than as an untested assumption in the provider. The example also carries a live acceptance script, so that it is proven by bringing the whole topology up and reaching it, not only by decoding its manifests and fitting them to their schemas. Two properties of the provider virtual DNS shape the manifests: a workload address table is written once at pod start, so a consumer that starts before its producer cannot reach it by cluster-local name, and WebSocket construction cannot fall back to discovery at all. The PDS crawler therefore points at the relay listener address, which needs no table lookup, while the relay reaches the PDS by the cluster-local name its own later start puts in the table. A fourth workspace, bob, carries a second PDS and the market's running bidder, so the topology exercises two independent OpenBao authorities and a workload that is not a TLS listener at all.

It also anchors the repo-level artifacts — module wiring, build entrypoint, and the ADRs and how-tos — that explain and reproduce how those resources are admitted, reconciled, and cancelled.
label: SpecContext
name: deno-kcp

intent: The context exists so that deno-kcp's architecture is a checked artifact rather than prose: arch.yaml states the repo's upstreams, kinds, boundaries, crossings, risks and reconcile passes, and validate.py is the gate that refuses a document whose ids, paths, symbols, boundary tree, crossing accounting or reconcile wiring do not hold together. It keeps the declared architecture in step with the Go source by checking kind names, resources, phases, conditions and status facts against the APIResourceSchema manifests and Go type files, and it keeps the document itself honest by rejecting duplicate YAML keys and schema nodes that lack descriptions.
label: SpecContext
name: tools-open-architecture

intent: This context exists so that the decision logic of a DenoRun lives in one place that can be tested without a cluster. The provider observes the cluster, builds the Observed value and applies the Result; the decider only decides, which keeps retries, deadlines, TTL cleanup and finalizer removal reviewable as pure rules. The context boundary is deliberate: no Kubernetes client, no side effects, no hidden state beyond Options, so a pass is reproducible from the observed facts alone.
label: SpecContext
name: internal-denorun

intent: This context exists to pin down the provider's process boundary: the single main that turns operator input (flags and environment) into the registry, engine runner, pod runner and provider the controller needs, and the failure and shutdown behaviour around them. Everything else in the repository assumes a configured provider already exists; this context is what makes one.
label: SpecContext
name: cmd-deno-kcp-provider

intent: This context exists so the PolicyWorkflowRun controller's state machine can be tested and reasoned about without a Kubernetes client: every decision is a pure function of an Observed snapshot, and the caller — internal/provider's reconcileWorkflowRun — owns the I/O that applies the returned Result. Keeping the decisions here means the ordering of teardown, cancellation, suspension, deadline, admission, start and observation handling is expressed in one place as data, rather than scattered across the reconciler's side effects.
label: SpecContext
name: internal-policyworkflowrun

intent: This context exists to hold the gate that decides whether a test requiring live infrastructure runs, fails or skips, so that ordinary runs stay green without the kcp, kine, kubectl and deno toolchain while a live-required run (DENO_KCP_REQUIRE_LIVE=1) cannot silently skip the live tests. It keeps that decision in one small exported surface, RequiresLive for callers that gate early, Require for callers that want fail-or-skip behavior, and Short for callers that additionally want the test to skip under go test -short.
label: SpecContext
name: internal-livegate

intent: This context exists so that DenoJob reconciliation has one place that decides and no place that acts: internal/provider observes the cluster and writes the Result back, while internal/denojob only turns observed state into a plan. Splitting the decision out keeps the job's phase, counters, conditions, requeue delay and delete flags testable without a client, and lets the provider layer stay a thin observer and writer.
label: SpecContext
name: internal-denojob

intent: This context exists so the PolicyEngine restart, readiness and liveness decisions live in one pure, separately testable place instead of being spread through the provider's reconcile loop. The provider observes the world (engine status, run state, probes, endpoint) and hands that snapshot to the decider; the decider returns the phase, run ID, ops and requeue delay it wants, and the provider is the only side that touches the cluster, the engine runner or the probe endpoints. That split keeps engine policy unit-testable through Observed values and keeps runner specifics out of the decision code.
label: SpecContext
name: internal-policyengine

intent: This context exists because the CRD types are the contract between the deno-kcp controllers and everything outside them: clients, informers and the denospec library all read these structs, so their field shape, phase vocabulary and deep-copy semantics must stay fixed and reviewable in one place. denospec.go is the bridge that keeps the Kubernetes-facing spelling of permissions and service accounts from drifting away from the library's own types.
label: SpecContext
name: api-v1alpha1

intent: This context exists so the repository can run a real OpenBao server from a single Go command with no external install, driven entirely by flags and environment variables. Integration tests and developers build and launch this binary, parse its readiness line to learn the URL and, in TLS mode, the generated CA path, then talk to the live server. The flag and environment surface, the root-token export, the TLS certificate directory handling, and the readiness line are therefore a contract that the tests depend on, and this document pins that contract.
label: SpecContext
name: internal-baoembed-cmd-baoembed
